Over the past few years, I've taken up some interest in the demographics of certain political views and affiliations. I'm currently interested in hearing the particulars in what causes people to change what were perhaps once deeply-seated affiliations. I have a few questions that I'd like answered, and your personal account(s) might help to shed some light on this.

Examples of the types of questions I have:

  1. Do most people switch from one extreme to another, or is it generally a gradual slide toward more moderate/centrist views?

  2. Do most people move toward more conservative views as they age, or do they become more centrist after a lifetime of experiences?

  3. How often does a change in political affiliation occur based on a change in religious views?

  4. How often does a change correlate to moving to a different geopolitical climate (from one country to another, or from an urban 'big progressive city' to rural 'small conservative town', etc)

------------ Warning: Below is essentially a personal rant. ------------

I'm interested in what you think, but I don't blame you for not proceeding.

Now at a personal level: I've admittedly changed political views from growing up in a conservative small town in the U.S. to substantially more moderate views after college. This seems to be a fairly typical transition, and I'd likely attribute that phenomenon to an expansion of inquisitive perspective through education. During my transition, I've noticed a ton of stereotypes for just about all walks of the political spectrum. In part, I'm also attempting to better understand which of them are substantiated and to what degree. And in so doing, I'm also trying to establish my own political identity from a more objective perspective.

Some observations of stereotypes of U.S. political affiliations: (Please feel free to add to this list or share your own country's list of stereotypes!)

  • Older people tend to be more likely to be conservative.
  • Isolated, rural areas tend to be more conservative, I'm guessing due to a homogenous population. (Essentially the same values, if you stand out by dressing differently or acting differently than everyone else, alarms go off.)
  • Larger cities seem to have a far more liberal climate, probably due to a mix of cultures which necessitates some level of open-mindedness.
  • Conservative republicans tend to have a higher degree of religious affiliation
  • Conservative republicans tend to value education less (I'm guessing this means gov't funded public education?)
  • Conservative republicans are rich white people
  • Republicans say, "I want to keep my money, not give it to the government"
  • Republicans are war mongers/aggressively pro-war, to a fault
  • Republicans are fascist oligarchs
  • Republicans are insane
  • Republicans go to ridiculous, ludicrous extremes to get what they want
  • Republican politicians only listen to rich bankrollers (seems to occur equally on both sides these days)
  • Libertarians/Republicans don't believe in a social safety net
  • Libertarians/Republicans seem to use the phrase "Well, who's going to pay for it?"
  • Libertarians (sometimes Republicans) don't care about the environment if it will bring in a profit
  • Libertarians seem to throw around the phrase "pragmatic solution" a lot
  • Libertarians are fascists
  • Libertarians are insane
  • The right is in an echo chamber and won't listen to reason
  • The left lives in la-la land and needs to be grounded in reality
  • The more educated a person becomes, the more liberal they tend to be
  • Democrats support bloated government and wasteful spending
  • Democrats are nothing but a big group of lazy welfare recipients who want the government to take care of them instead of working
  • Democrats are anti-war liberal pussies
  • Liberals are retarded

Using my imagination, I can -to a point- understand why people believe in what they do, in that people 'have their reasons'. At this point, I'm really only trying to establish my own political identity from an objective perspective. It seems like the political climate has become very pushy; people seem more polarized than ever and bipartisanship is all but gone except for when something benefits the wealthy. I also feel like our country's identity has become increasingly morally bankrupt, and our political system and media have become entirely corrupted by money (not a new idea, but it's really coming to a head). I've been looking into WolfPAC, and I really hope it gains traction.

In short, I don't know what to do. So far the best thing I've found is to not watch any cable network news. The next safest thing is to not talk to anyone about politics because many people seem to have such a strong, polarized opinion, and often they seem to take any deviation from their views as some sort of personal insult or ideological threat. It's a shit-show that I'd rather avoid, but I really enjoy centrist political discussion with the ability to entertain a devils advocate. I feel like this is healthy, and our political discourse has become so poisoned that it might as well be considered a faux pas to bring up politics in nearly any social setting.

Edit: What was the right's like?

Well, I spent a lot of my childhood in the tractor with my grandpa, who always had Bill O'Reilly and Sean Hannity playing on the radio. I was indoctrinated in a fairly strict-ish Christian church (Think 'Catholic Lite'). We were more or less taught that rich people earned their money, and that politicians should believe in God, and if they do, they will make the right choices for us. Should you be called upon, fighting and dying for your religious beliefs was expected of you. It wasn't militant -- we weren't given a bible and an M16 when we turned 8 or anything like that -- but the declaration was part of it. Conservatism was the name of the game; bringing up new ideas or questioning old ones was generally frowned upon. Long hair on males wasn't socially acceptable, and if a guy came home with his ear pierced it would get ripped from his ear lobe. If you wanted to stand out, it had better only be on the football field or basketball court. And this was during the 90's-00's.

I started gaining perspective my 2-3rd year of college. I remember being pissed off my freshman year when a professor more or less told us that religion is nothing more than an institution, something that keeps individuals cohesive in a community and (generally) under control. I remember watching Fox News and then seeing MSNBC/CNN and wondering how the other news networks could get the same story so wrong. You know, how could an entire news network possibly be so dumb and short-sighted? It was baffling, until I read more, witnessed more, and learned more. Then like you, I also became depressed. It was really strange, feeling like your whole basis for reality wasn't actually there. It was all invented by other people, who might or might not be any more correct than anyone else with similar or dissimilar ideas. It was a real wake-up call.

Then I kinda said 'fuck it' for a few years and just started studying more about hard sciences, mainly astrophysics, cosmology and theoretical physics on one side and neuroscience and neurophilosophy on the other. That helped a lot; once I started peering behind the curtain of nature, I realized how small peoples ideas were when they involved things like politics, religion, celebrity gossip/pop-culture. It was originally terrifying to understand that entire populations live within these artificial constructs. Discovering the level of strategy and manipulation that goes into media itself...it was mind-bending. But once I realized that it was what people did when they had nothing 'better' to do, like challenge themselves with discovering truths of the natural universe, it was easier for me to disregard those things. But I hated people for buying into it, and really hated people for expecting others to buy into their belief systems/points of view/moral constructs/etc. Now I'm kinda stuck sitting here, wondering about the human condition and what's next. I don't feel superior because I don't have all the answers, and I feel a bit alienated because I denounced a lot of the 'essence' of what my past was built upon. It's depressingly lonely, but I suppose somewhat liberating.

Looking back, it was sort of an accidental bible->Chomsky->Freud->Spinoza->Kierkegaard->Nietzsche progression, I guess. With intermittent Aristotle/Plato and a some Hegel and Sartre thrown in the mix. These days, Buddhism is starting to make a lot of sense because it seems...mentally objective. I just need to pick the next philosophy in line and keep learning, I guess.
